question: How does the copper price reach Freeport-McMoRan's cash flow, and what held its volumes back in 2026?

summary.text: In the third quarter of 2026 Freeport-McMoRan sold {{r3-cu-sales-q3-2026}} of copper on its consolidated basis, against {{r3-cu-sales-q3-2025}} a year earlier; the company names lower operating rates at PTFI while the Grasberg Block Cave mine ramps up after the September 2025 mud rush.

In the company's revenue bridge for the quarter, the volume lines of the three metals ({{c-rev-bridge-volume-q3-2026|signed}}) outweighed the price lines ({{c-rev-bridge-price-q3-2026|signed}}), yet revenue rose on its other lines.
In November the board approved a {{nr-bagdad-capex-estimate}} expansion of the Bagdad mine in Arizona; its cost, output and timing are company estimates.

summary_more.text: Freeport-McMoRan mines copper in the United States, Peru and Chile, and Indonesia; copper was {{k25-revenue-share-copper-fy2025}} of its consolidated revenues in 2025.

The largest of the other revenue lines was Atlantic Copper, the Spanish smelter ({{q3-rev-bridge-atlantic-q3-2026|signed}}), whose copper purchases also raised costs; lower export duties added {{q3-rev-bridge-export-duties-q3-2026|signed}}.
Unit net cash costs rose to {{r3-cu-unc-q3-2026}} a pound, from {{r3-cu-unc-q3-2025}}; they leave out mud-rush idle costs of {{q3-idle-pd-per-lb-q3-2026}} a pound.

Operating cash flows for the first nine months of 2026 were {{r3-ocf-9m-2026}}, including {{r3-cf-insurance-9m-2026}} of insurance proceeds. For the same months of 2025 the 10-Q shows {{q3-ocf-9m-2025}} and the release {{r3-ocf-9m-2025}}; neither explains the difference.

FCX's share of consolidated net income rose to {{c-common-share-ni-q3-2026}}, from {{c-common-share-ni-q3-2025}}: Indonesia, where FCX owns {{r3-ptfi-ownership}}, earned less. The company names this beside prices and lower taxes, without saying how much each explains.

note.text: Leaves out mud-rush idle costs of {{q3-idle-pd-per-lb-q3-2026}} a pound.

The company's plan: eighty percent of capacity in mid-2027, near full capacity by the end of 2027.

The largest other line is Atlantic Copper, the Spanish smelter ({{q3-rev-bridge-atlantic-q3-2026|signed}}). The company's reason for higher production costs starts with its copper purchases, so that revenue came with costs.
Lower export duties added {{q3-rev-bridge-export-duties-q3-2026|signed}}. Duties were charged on concentrate exports until the export licence expired in September 2025.
The full bridge is under Numbers. The grouping into volume, price and other lines is this project's; the lines are the company's.

changes.text: Unit net cash costs rose by {{c-chg-cu-unc-q3-2026}} a pound, to {{r3-cu-unc-q3-2026}} a pound.

detail.text: They leave out mud-rush idle facility, recovery and restoration costs: {{r3-idle-costs-q3-2026}} in the quarter, or {{q3-idle-pd-per-lb-q3-2026}} a pound.
While the ramp-up lasts, read the excluded idle costs beside the unit cost. Adding the two is this project's arithmetic, not a company measure.

changes.text: Operating cash flows were {{r3-ocf-q3-2026}} ({{c-yoy-ocf-q3-2026|signed}}); FCX's share of consolidated net income rose to {{c-common-share-ni-q3-2026}}, from {{c-common-share-ni-q3-2025}}.

detail.text: Cash used for working capital rose in the quarter.

The share of profit moves with the mix: Indonesia, where FCX owns {{r3-ptfi-ownership}}, earned less, and the wholly owned U.S. mines earned more. The company names this beside prices and lower taxes, without saying how much each explains.

reading_guide.text: Quarter, nine-month and annual figures sit in separate columns, and a change is only shown between periods of the same length.

Consolidated figures include all of PTFI, Cerro Verde and El Abra, though FCX owns {{r3-ptfi-ownership}}, {{r3-cerro-verde-ownership}} and {{k25-ownership-el-abra}} of them. Figures attributable to common stock are FCX shareholders' part, and they are labelled.

Nine-month operating income and operating cash flows include a one-off insurance settlement of {{r3-cf-insurance-9m-2026}}. Without it, nine-month operating cash flows would be {{c-ocf-ex-insurance-9m-2026}}, which is this project's arithmetic.

blocks.text: Revenue in 2025: copper {{k25-revenue-share-copper-fy2025}}, gold {{k25-revenue-share-gold-fy2025}}, molybdenum {{k25-revenue-share-molybdenum-fy2025}}.

Copper production in 2025: the United States {{k25-prod-alloc-copper-us-fy2025}}, South America {{k25-prod-alloc-copper-south-america-fy2025}}, Indonesia {{k25-prod-alloc-copper-indonesia-fy2025}}. Indonesia produced {{k25-prod-alloc-gold-indonesia-fy2025}} of the gold.
In the United States FCX is the leading copper supplier.

When that inventory is sold it should return cash; when depends on the smelter ramp-up and on the gold export question.

intro.text: Two separate calculations on the company's assumptions for the fourth quarter of 2026. Change an input and see what changes in each. Neither is a projection of this project's, a valuation or a reported result, and the two are never added together.

base.label: Copper sold in the quarter (sales, not production)

base_value.label: Price × volume at the company's assumptions

definition.text: Price × volume: an approximate value of copper sales under these assumptions. It is not reported revenue, earnings or cash flow.

method.text: The change is split in one fixed order: the volume effect is the change in pounds valued at the company's price, and the price effect is the change in price on your volume. The two always add up to the change; another order would split it differently.

sources.text: The company's copper price for the fourth quarter, {{r3-out-cu-price-q4-2026}} a pound, is the price its 2026 outlook assumes.
The company's copper sales for the fourth quarter: {{r3-out-cu-sales-q4-2026}}.

costs.text: The 10-K says a significant portion of PTFI's costs are fixed and its unit costs vary with volumes.
These documents give no split of costs into fixed and variable, and no bridge from volume to operating cash flows.

So a change in volume is not carried to cash flow here. Holding the cost per pound constant while volume changes would treat every cost as variable, which the 10-K says is not so at PTFI; for the other mines these documents give no split either way.

base.label: Change in operating cash flows for each step
Step in the average copper price

definition.text: The company's figure: each {{r3-sens-ocf-copper-step}} a pound change in the average copper price during the fourth quarter of 2026 would change consolidated operating cash flows for the year 2026 by about {{r3-sens-ocf-copper}}, at its current sales volume and cost estimates.

linear.text: Multiplying that figure by your price change is this project's linear use of the company's approximate figure. The company gives it for each step around {{r3-out-cu-price-q4-2026}} a pound and does not say over what range of prices it holds.

held.text: Volumes, costs and the company's other assumptions stay as the company states them; only the average copper price in the fourth quarter moves.

not_used.text: A change in volume from the first calculation is not added here: the company publishes no figure for how cash flows move with volume.
The 10-K's older sensitivity, for a price change across all of 2026 at its February assumptions, is not used: it belongs to another period, price level and volume.

versus.text: At the company's volume, a {{r3-sens-ocf-copper-step}} move in price adds {{c-q4-copper-revenue-per-10c}} to price × volume for the quarter, while the company's figure for operating cash flows is {{r3-sens-ocf-copper}}. They measure different things. The company does not split the difference, so this page does not put it down to taxes, royalties, a cost or timing.
